course.title: Developmental Psychology
course.description: Developmental psychology is the scientific study of how and why people change across the whole lifespan, from the womb through old age. This course walks through the big debates and theories - nature and nurture, research methods, Piaget, Vygotsky, attachment, Erikson, moral reasoning, and aging - in plain language with worked examples. Its structure is informed by the Developmental Psychology article on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: Developmental psychology is best described as the study of...
options: how and why people change across the entire lifespan
the structure of the adult brain alone
how to treat mental illness in adults
questions.explanation: Developmental psychology studies how and why people change from conception through old age, not just childhood.

questions.prompt: The nature versus nurture debate asks whether development is driven mainly by...
options: genes and biology versus experience and environment
questions.explanation: Nature is inherited biology; nurture is experience and environment. Modern research says the two interact.

questions.prompt: A study that follows the same group of people over many years is called...
questions.explanation: Following the same people over time is a longitudinal design; testing different ages at once is cross-sectional.

questions.prompt: A baby who understands that a hidden toy still exists has developed...
questions.explanation: Knowing a hidden object still exists is object permanence, a hallmark of Piaget's sensorimotor stage.

questions.prompt: The gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with help is Vygotsky's...
questions.explanation: That gap is Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, the target of good teaching and scaffolding.

questions.prompt: Ainsworth's Strange Situation procedure was designed to measure...
options: the quality of a child's attachment
questions.explanation: The Strange Situation measures the quality of attachment through a series of separations and reunions.

questions.prompt: According to Erikson, the central task of adolescence is...
questions.explanation: Erikson placed identity versus role confusion in adolescence, the search for a stable sense of self.
Kohlberg studied how moral reasoning develops through preconventional, conventional, and postconventional levels.

lessons.title: What developmental psychology studies: nature and nurture
lessons.grammar_note: Nature and nurture interact rather than compete, so describe influences as working together, not as one winning out over the other.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what developmental psychology studies and frame any change you see as a mix of nature and nurture rather than one or the other. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, is development only about childhood, or does it run the whole lifespan? By the end of this lesson you should be able to define the field in one sentence, give an everyday example of a biological influence and an environmental influence on the same behavior, and say why most modern researchers treat the old either-or question as the wrong question. You will also be ready to spot when a headline overclaims that a single gene or a single experience causes a complex outcome, and to translate such claims into the more careful language of interacting influences that the field actually uses.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Developmental psychology is the scientific study of how and why human beings change over the course of their lives. It once focused mainly on infants and children, but today it covers the entire lifespan, including adolescence, adult development, and aging. Researchers look at physical growth, thinking and problem solving, language, emotion, personality, and social relationships, and they ask both how a capacity appears and why it develops as it does. A central organizing question is nature versus nurture: how much of who we become is shaped by inherited biology (genes, maturation, temperament) and how much by experience (family, culture, learning, nutrition). The modern answer is that the two are deeply intertwined. Genes set ranges and tendencies, environments switch them on or off and shape how they are expressed, and the two interact continuously. Few outcomes are purely one or the other.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Early baby biographers such as Charles Darwin kept detailed diaries of their own infants, and Darwin's 1877 sketch of an infant helped launch systematic child study. G. Stanley Hall founded child study in the United States and popularized the scientific study of adolescence. Arnold Gesell documented maturational milestones, stressing biological timetables on the nature side. On the nurture side, John Watson argued behavior is shaped by learning, famously claiming he could train any healthy infant into any profession. Later the field moved beyond the either-or frame. Modern behavioral genetics and the study of gene-environment interaction, along with work on epigenetics, show inherited and experiential factors shaping each other. Konrad Lorenz's work on imprinting in birds also highlighted critical or sensitive periods, windows when experience has an outsized effect on a biologically prepared system.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Define developmental psychology in one sentence. 2) Give one biological and one environmental influence on height. 3) True or false: development stops at the end of childhood. 4) What does gene-environment interaction mean? 5) Why do researchers say nature versus nurture is the wrong framing? Answers: 1) The scientific study of how and why people change across the lifespan. 2) Biological: inherited genes for height; environmental: childhood nutrition. 3) False - it continues through adulthood and old age. 4) Genes and experiences influence each other, so the effect of one depends on the other. 5) Because almost every outcome reflects both working together, not one acting alone.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming developmental psychology is only about babies and young children, when it spans the whole lifespan. Mistake: treating nature and nurture as a tug-of-war with a single winner, when they interact. Mistake: reading a phrase like a gene for a trait as meaning one gene fully determines a complex outcome. Exit: (a) Does development end in childhood? (b) In one phrase, how do nature and nurture relate? Answers: no, it continues across the entire lifespan; they interact continuously, each shaping how the other is expressed.

lessons.title: How we study development: cross-sectional and longitudinal methods
lessons.grammar_note: Keep them straight: cross-sectional compares different ages at one point in time, while longitudinal follows the same people over time.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Tell apart the main research designs developmental psychologists use, and in particular contrast cross-sectional and longitudinal studies, naming a strength and a weakness of each. Warm-up: if you wanted to know how memory changes from age 20 to age 70, would you rather test many ages once, or follow one group for fifty years? By the end you should be able to match a research question to a suitable design, explain why a correlation does not prove causation, and recognize the cohort problem that can distort age comparisons. You should also be able to say why researchers sometimes combine designs, and why studying children raises special ethical concerns.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: To study change over time, researchers choose a design. A cross-sectional study tests people of different ages at the same point in time, for example comparing 5, 10, and 15 year olds this year. It is fast and cheap, but it confuses age with cohort: the groups grew up in different eras, so a difference might reflect history, not development. A longitudinal study follows the same people repeatedly over months or years. It shows genuine change within individuals, but it is slow, expensive, and loses participants over time, a problem called attrition. A sequential design combines both to capture the strengths of each. Beyond these, researchers use experiments, which can show cause and effect by manipulating a variable, along with correlational studies, which measure relationships but cannot prove cause, plus case studies and naturalistic observation. Ethics matter especially with children, who cannot fully consent.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Longitudinal research has a long pedigree. Lewis Terman began a famous longitudinal study of gifted children in 1921 that followed participants for decades. The idea of combining designs to separate age, cohort, and time-of-measurement effects was developed by K. Warner Schaie, whose Seattle Longitudinal Study of adult intelligence is a landmark of the sequential approach. Jean Piaget relied heavily on close observation and the clinical interview, watching and questioning children, including his own, to infer how they think. Naturalistic observation and structured tasks remain core tools across the field. Over time the shift has been toward designs and statistics that let researchers draw firmer conclusions about what truly changes with age versus what merely differs between generations, and toward stronger ethical safeguards for young participants.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which design tests different ages at one time? 2) Which design follows the same people over years? 3) Name one weakness of cross-sectional studies. 4) Name one weakness of longitudinal studies. 5) Does a correlation between screen time and grades prove screens cause lower grades? Answers: 1) Cross-sectional. 2) Longitudinal. 3) Cohort effects - the age groups differ by generation, not just by age. 4) Slow, costly, and prone to participant drop-out (attrition). 5) No - correlation does not prove causation; a third factor could explain both.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading an age difference in a cross-sectional study as proof of developmental change, ignoring that the groups are different generations. Mistake: assuming a correlation means one thing causes the other. Mistake: forgetting that attrition can bias a longitudinal sample if the people who drop out differ from those who stay. Exit: (a) Which design best shows change within the same individuals over time? (b) What does a cross-sectional study confuse age with? Answers: longitudinal; cohort or generation.

lessons.title: Prenatal development and infancy
lessons.grammar_note: Order the prenatal stages germinal, then embryonic, then fetal - the major organs take shape in the embryonic stage.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Outline the three stages of prenatal development, name key milestones of the first two years, and explain why early sensitive periods and teratogens matter. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what capacity lets a baby know a hidden toy still exists? By the end you should be able to put the germinal, embryonic, and fetal stages in order, describe how newborn reflexes and senses work, list several motor and perceptual milestones of infancy, and give an example of a teratogen and the harm it can cause. You should also be able to explain why both the timing and the dose of an exposure shape its effect on the developing child.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Prenatal development unfolds in three stages. The germinal stage, roughly the first two weeks, runs from conception through implantation of the zygote. The embryonic stage, about weeks three to eight, is when major organs and body systems form, a time of rapid growth and high vulnerability. The fetal stage, week nine to birth, brings growth, movement, and maturation of the organs. Teratogens, harmful agents such as alcohol, certain drugs, some infections, and radiation, can disrupt development, with timing and dose shaping the damage. Newborns arrive with reflexes such as rooting, sucking, and grasping, and with surprisingly capable senses, especially hearing and a preference for faces. Across infancy, motor skills follow a broadly predictable order of head control, sitting, crawling, and walking, while perception, memory, and early thinking advance quickly, setting the stage for later cognitive growth.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: The study of teratogens grew sharply after the thalidomide tragedy of the late 1950s and early 1960s, when a morning-sickness drug caused severe limb malformations, showing how a single agent at a sensitive time can alter development. Research on fetal alcohol spectrum disorders later documented the lasting harm of prenatal alcohol exposure. In infancy research, Robert Fantz pioneered looking-time methods in the 1960s, showing that even very young babies prefer to look at faces and patterned stimuli, which revealed that newborns perceive far more than once assumed. Later researchers used habituation and violation-of-expectation tasks to probe what infants know. This work pushed estimates of infant competence far earlier than Piaget's original timetable suggested.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Put the prenatal stages in order. 2) During which stage do the major organs first form? 3) What is a teratogen? 4) Name two newborn reflexes. 5) Give the usual order of these milestones: walking, sitting, crawling. Answers: 1) Germinal, embryonic, fetal. 2) The embryonic stage. 3) A harmful agent that can disrupt prenatal development, such as alcohol. 4) Any two of rooting, sucking, grasping. 5) Sitting, then crawling, then walking.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking the fetus is fully formed early, when major organs take shape in the embryonic stage and the fetal stage is mostly growth and maturation. Mistake: assuming newborns sense little, when hearing and a face preference are present at birth. Mistake: believing any amount of a teratogen is equally safe or equally harmful, when timing and dose both matter. Exit: (a) Which prenatal stage is most vulnerable to organ malformation? (b) Name one teratogen. Answers: the embryonic stage; alcohol (or thalidomide, or certain infections).

lessons.title: Piaget's stages and the growth of moral reasoning
lessons.grammar_note: Piaget's stages run sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational - concrete comes before formal, and conservation marks the concrete stage.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name Piaget's four stages of cognitive development in order and link them to Kohlberg's levels of moral reasoning. Warm-up: a child who thinks a tall thin glass holds more juice than a short wide one is missing which concept? By the end you should be able to list the sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, and formal operational stages with one hallmark of each, explain conservation and egocentrism, and describe Kohlberg's three levels of moral thinking and how they build on Piaget's stage approach. You should also be able to explain why Kohlberg scored the reasoning behind a choice rather than the choice itself.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Jean Piaget proposed that children actively build knowledge through schemas, adjusting them by assimilation, which fits new input into existing ideas, and accommodation, which changes ideas to fit new input. He described four stages. In the sensorimotor stage, birth to about 2, infants learn through senses and action and gain object permanence. In the preoperational stage, about 2 to 7, children use symbols and language but are egocentric and lack conservation, failing to grasp that quantity stays the same despite changes in shape. In the concrete operational stage, about 7 to 11, logical thinking about concrete things appears, including conservation. In the formal operational stage, about 11 and up, abstract and hypothetical reasoning becomes possible. Lawrence Kohlberg extended this stage approach to morality, proposing that moral reasoning advances through preconventional, conventional, and postconventional levels.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Jean Piaget, a Swiss scholar, built his theory from close observation and clever tasks, such as the conservation-of-liquid test and hiding games that reveal object permanence. His work, from the 1920s onward, reshaped how we understand children's thinking, though later researchers found he often underestimated young children. Lawrence Kohlberg, writing in the 1950s and after, studied moral reasoning by posing dilemmas, most famously the Heinz dilemma, about whether a man should steal an overpriced drug to save his wife. Kohlberg cared less about the yes-or-no answer than about the reasoning behind it, which he sorted into six stages across three levels. Carol Gilligan later criticized Kohlberg's framework for emphasizing justice over an ethic of care, and for drawing early conclusions mainly from male participants.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) List Piaget's four stages in order. 2) What is object permanence, and in which stage does it develop? 3) What is conservation? 4) Name Kohlberg's three levels. 5) In the Heinz dilemma, what did Kohlberg actually score? Answers: 1) Sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational. 2) Knowing a hidden object still exists; the sensorimotor stage. 3) Understanding that quantity stays the same despite changes in appearance. 4) Preconventional, conventional, postconventional. 5) The reasoning behind the answer, not the answer itself.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: swapping the order of the concrete and formal operational stages, when concrete comes first. Mistake: thinking conservation appears in the preoperational stage, when it marks the concrete operational stage. Mistake: scoring Kohlberg's dilemmas by the choice made rather than the justification given. Exit: (a) In which stage does conservation appear? (b) Does Kohlberg's level depend on the answer or the reasoning? Answers: the concrete operational stage; the reasoning.

questions.prompt: Most modern researchers see development as driven by...
options: an interaction of nature and nurture
questions.explanation: Modern research treats development as an interaction of genes and environment, not one acting alone.

questions.prompt: A study that follows the same people over many years is...
questions.explanation: A longitudinal study follows the same people over time, showing change within individuals.

questions.prompt: During which prenatal stage do the major organs first form?
questions.explanation: Major organs form during the embryonic stage, about weeks 3 to 8, the most vulnerable period.

questions.prompt: In Piaget's theory, knowing that a hidden object still exists is...
questions.explanation: Object permanence is the understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight.

questions.prompt: Conservation first appears in which Piagetian stage?
questions.explanation: Conservation marks the concrete operational stage, not the earlier preoperational stage.

questions.prompt: Kohlberg's dilemmas, such as the Heinz dilemma, were scored based on...
questions.explanation: Kohlberg scored the reasoning behind the choice, which revealed the level of moral thinking.

lessons.title: Vygotsky, sociocultural theory, and language development
lessons.grammar_note: Vygotsky is social (learning with more knowledgeable others); Piaget is individual (the child acting largely alone).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain Vygotsky's sociocultural view of development and connect it to how children acquire language. Warm-up: what is the gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with help called? By the end you should be able to define the zone of proximal development and scaffolding, contrast Vygotsky with Piaget, outline the typical milestones of early language from cooing through babbling, first words, and telegraphic speech, and summarize the long-running debate between nativist and learning accounts of how children acquire grammar so quickly. You should also be able to explain how private speech, children talking to themselves, relates to later inner thought.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Lev Vygotsky argued that development is fundamentally social. Children learn through interaction with more knowledgeable others such as parents, teachers, and peers, and they gradually internalize the tools of their culture, above all language. His key idea is the zone of proximal development: the range of tasks a child cannot yet do alone but can do with guidance. Good teaching aims at that zone and provides scaffolding, temporary support that is withdrawn as skill grows. Where Piaget saw a lone scientist building knowledge through action, Vygotsky saw a social apprentice guided by others. Language development fits this view. Infants coo, then babble, say first words around one year, combine words into two-word telegraphic speech by about age two, and then expand rapidly. Private speech, children talking themselves through tasks, later turns inward and becomes inner thought.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Lev Vygotsky, a Russian psychologist of the 1920s and 1930s, died young, and his work reached the West decades later, where it reshaped education through ideas like scaffolding, a term coined by Jerome Bruner and colleagues. On language, Noam Chomsky argued that children are born with an innate capacity for grammar, since they learn language far faster than simple imitation and reward could explain, a nativist view he set against B. F. Skinner's behaviorist account of language as learned through reinforcement. Eric Lenneberg proposed a critical period for language. Researchers also point to child-directed speech and the role of social interaction, echoing Vygotsky, in helping children crack the code of their native tongue and move from single words to full sentences.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Define the zone of proximal development. 2) What is scaffolding? 3) How does Vygotsky differ from Piaget? 4) Put in order: babbling, first words, telegraphic speech, cooing. 5) What did Chomsky claim about grammar? Answers: 1) The gap between what a child can do alone and what they can do with help. 2) Temporary guided support that is reduced as the learner improves. 3) Vygotsky stresses social interaction and culture; Piaget stresses the child acting alone. 4) Cooing, babbling, first words, telegraphic speech. 5) That children have an innate, built-in capacity for grammar.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating the zone of proximal development as a fixed trait rather than a moving range that shifts as the child learns. Mistake: thinking scaffolding means doing the task for the child, when it means supporting and then stepping back. Mistake: assuming language is learned purely by imitation, which cannot explain its speed and creativity. Exit: (a) Who emphasized the social and cultural roots of thinking? (b) What is the term for temporary, fading support? Answers: Vygotsky; scaffolding.

lessons.title: Attachment: Bowlby, Ainsworth, and the Strange Situation
lessons.grammar_note: In the Strange Situation, read the reunion, not the separation, to judge how secure a child's attachment is.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain attachment theory, describe the Strange Situation, and name the main attachment patterns and what they predict. Warm-up: what procedure did Ainsworth design to measure a child's attachment? By the end you should be able to state Bowlby's core claim that infants are biologically prepared to bond with caregivers, describe how the Strange Situation works, distinguish secure from insecure patterns, and explain what a secure base is and why sensitive, consistent caregiving matters. You should also be able to say why the reunion, rather than the separation, is the most revealing part of the procedure, and what Harlow's monkey studies added to the picture.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Attachment is the deep emotional bond between an infant and a caregiver. John Bowlby argued it is biologically built in: infants are prepared to seek closeness to caregivers, because staying near a protector aided survival. A responsive caregiver becomes a secure base from which the child explores and a safe haven to return to when distressed. Mary Ainsworth created the Strange Situation, a structured lab procedure with a series of separations and reunions, to measure the quality of this bond. From infants' reactions, especially at reunion, she identified patterns. Securely attached infants use the caregiver as a base, protest at separation, and are comforted at reunion. Insecure patterns include avoidant, with little visible reaction, and resistant or ambivalent, where the child is hard to soothe. A later disorganized pattern shows confused, contradictory behavior. Sensitive, consistent caregiving tends to predict secure attachment.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: John Bowlby, drawing on ethology and his observations of children separated from parents, set out attachment theory in influential work from the 1950s and 1960s, including reports for the World Health Organization on maternal deprivation. Mary Ainsworth, who worked with Bowlby, developed the Strange Situation in the 1970s and conducted detailed home observations in Uganda and Baltimore, linking caregiver sensitivity to attachment security. Harry Harlow's experiments with infant monkeys and cloth versus wire surrogate mothers showed that comfort contact, not just feeding, drives bonding, undercutting the view that infants love whoever feeds them. Later, Mary Main and colleagues identified the disorganized pattern and developed interview methods for studying attachment across the lifespan.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is a secure base? 2) Who designed the Strange Situation? 3) Name two insecure attachment patterns. 4) What did Harlow's monkey studies show? 5) Why, in Bowlby's view, did attachment evolve? Answers: 1) A trusted caregiver from whom a child explores and to whom they return when upset. 2) Mary Ainsworth. 3) Avoidant and resistant or ambivalent (also disorganized). 4) That comfort contact matters more than feeding for bonding. 5) Because staying close to a protective caregiver improved an infant's chances of survival.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking attachment is just about who feeds the baby, when Harlow showed comfort contact matters more. Mistake: reading the Strange Situation mainly from the separation rather than the reunion, which is most telling. Mistake: assuming a secure base means a clingy child, when secure infants actually explore more freely. Exit: (a) Who proposed that attachment is biologically built in? (b) What does a securely attached infant do at reunion? Answers: John Bowlby; seeks and is comforted by the caregiver, then returns to play.

lessons.title: Erikson across the lifespan: adolescence, adulthood, and aging
lessons.grammar_note: Keep the order: adolescence is identity versus role confusion; young adulthood is intimacy versus isolation - do not swap them.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe Erikson's lifespan theory of psychosocial stages and apply it to adolescence, adulthood, and old age. Warm-up: according to Erikson, what is the central conflict of adolescence? By the end you should be able to explain that Erikson saw development as a series of conflicts across the whole life, name the central conflicts of adolescence, young adulthood, middle adulthood, and old age, and connect these to real changes such as identity, relationships, generativity, and the physical and cognitive shifts of aging. You should also be able to distinguish which mental abilities tend to decline with age from those that are usually well preserved.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Erik Erikson proposed eight psychosocial stages, each centered on a conflict the person must resolve. Unlike theories that stop at childhood, his spans the entire lifespan. Infancy brings trust versus mistrust, then autonomy versus shame, initiative versus guilt, and industry versus inferiority through childhood. Adolescence brings identity versus role confusion, the search for a stable sense of self. Young adulthood centers on intimacy versus isolation, forming close bonds. Middle adulthood turns on generativity versus stagnation, contributing to the next generation through work, parenting, or mentoring. Old age brings integrity versus despair, looking back on life with acceptance or regret. Aging also involves real physical change and shifts in cognition. Some abilities, such as processing speed and certain kinds of memory, tend to decline, while others, such as vocabulary and accumulated knowledge, often hold steady or even grow.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Erik Erikson, a developmental thinker influenced by but departing from Freud, laid out his eight stages in Childhood and Society in 1950, and developed the concept of the identity crisis in adolescence. His collaborator and wife, Joan Erikson, later extended the model to very old age. On aging specifically, researchers distinguish fluid intelligence, which is reasoning with novel problems and tends to decline, from crystallized intelligence, which is knowledge and vocabulary and is well preserved, an idea from Raymond Cattell and John Horn. Work on successful aging and on conditions such as dementia rounds out the lifespan picture. The key shift Erikson helped drive was treating adulthood and old age as periods of genuine development, not merely decline after a childhood peak.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the central conflict of adolescence in Erikson's theory? 2) What conflict defines young adulthood? 3) What is generativity? 4) Which type of intelligence tends to hold up well in old age? 5) How many psychosocial stages did Erikson propose? Answers: 1) Identity versus role confusion. 2) Intimacy versus isolation. 3) Contributing to the next generation, through work, parenting, or mentoring. 4) Crystallized intelligence, meaning knowledge and vocabulary. 5) Eight.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking Erikson's stages cover only childhood, when they run from infancy to old age. Mistake: assuming all mental abilities decline with age, when crystallized knowledge often holds or grows. Mistake: confusing identity, the task of adolescence, with intimacy, the task of young adulthood. Exit: (a) What conflict marks old age in Erikson's theory? (b) Name one ability that tends to be preserved in aging. Answers: integrity versus despair; vocabulary or accumulated knowledge (crystallized intelligence).

items.example: A longitudinal study might test the same children's memory every year from age 5 to 15.

items.translation: a harmful agent that can disrupt prenatal development
items.example: Alcohol is a teratogen; heavy prenatal exposure can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders.
